claim: Summation of ionotropic receptor-mediated responses is critical in neuronal computation by shaping input-output characteristics of neurons.
source: Summation of ionotropic receptor-mediated responses is critical in neuronal computation by shaping input-output characteristics of neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of ionotropic receptor summation, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Arithmetics of summation for metabotropic signals are not known.
source: However, arithmetics of summation for metabotropic signals are not known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge about metabotropic signal summation.

claim: Triple recordings from presynaptic NGFCs converging to a postsynaptic neuron revealed sublinear summation of ionotropic GABAA responses.
source: Triple recordings from presynaptic NGFCs converging to a postsynaptic neuron revealed sublinear summation of ionotropic GABAA responses and linear summation of metabotropic GABAB responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings described in the manuscript.

claim: Triple recordings from presynaptic NGFCs converging to a postsynaptic neuron revealed linear summation of metabotropic GABAB responses.
source: Triple recordings from presynaptic NGFCs converging to a postsynaptic neuron revealed sublinear summation of ionotropic GABAA responses and linear summation of metabotropic GABAB responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings described in the manuscript.

claim: In 83% of cases one or two NGFCs can provide input to a point in the neuropil.
source: Based on a model combining properties of volume transmission and distributions of all NGFC axon terminals, we predict that in 83% of cases one or two NGFCs can provide input to a point in the neuropil.
evidence: This prediction is based on computational modeling incorporating experimental data on NGFC axon distributions.

claim: Interactions of metabotropic GABAergic responses remain linear even if most superficial layer interneurons specialized to recruit GABAB receptors are simultaneously active.
source: We suggest that interactions of metabotropic GABAergic responses remain linear even if most superficial layer interneurons specialized to recruit GABAB receptors are simultaneously active.
evidence: This suggestion is based on experimental findings and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synchronization of GABAergic inputs appears to be crucial in structuring cellular and network excitation and behaviorally relevant rhythmic population activity.
source: Synchronization of GABAergic inputs appears to be crucial in structuring cellular and network excitation and behaviorally relevant rhythmic population activity (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Diverse subpopulations of GABAergic neurons contribute to network mechanisms at different temporal windows.
source: Diverse subpopulations of GABAergic neurons contribute to network mechanisms at different temporal windows and synchronized cells of particular interneuron types appear to fire in a stereotyped fashion (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Synchronized cells of particular interneuron types appear to fire in a stereotyped fashion.
source: Diverse subpopulations of GABAergic neurons contribute to network mechanisms at different temporal windows and synchronized cells of particular interneuron types appear to fire in a stereotyped fashion (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Coactivation of similar GABAergic inputs frequently results from synchronization of particular interneuron types.
source: In general, this frequently results in coactivation of similar (and asynchronization of dissimilar) GABAergic inputs arriving to target neurons (Jang et al., 2020; Karnani et al., 2016; Kvitsiani et al., 2013), which leads to postsynaptic summation of GABAergic responses synchronously activated by presynaptic cells of the same type.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Most GABAergic cell types exert inhibitory control through ionotropic GABAA receptors allowing Cl− ions to pass rapidly through the membrane.
source: Most GABAergic cell types exert inhibitory control through ionotropic GABAA receptors allowing Cl− ions to pass rapidly through the membrane (Barker and Ransom, 1978) and depending on the magnitude of GABA release and/or the number of synchronously active presynaptic interneurons, synaptic and extrasynaptic GABAA receptors could be recruited.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The integration of ionotropic inhibitory signals on the surface of target cell dendrites is temporally precise and spatially specific.
source: The integration of ionotropic inhibitory signals on the surface of target cell dendrites is temporally precise and spatially specific (Bloss et al., 2016; Klausberger, 2009; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Summation of ionotropic receptor-mediated responses are predominantly characterized by nonlinear rules of interaction in the neocortex.
source: Summation of ionotropic receptor-mediated responses are extensively studied in the neocortex and predominantly characterized by nonlinear rules of interaction (Jadi et al., 2012; Koch et al., 1983; London and Häusser, 2005; Qian and Sejnowski, 1990; Silver, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Metabotropic GABAB receptor activation can occur during synchronized and/or long-lasting activation of GABAergic inputs.
source: In addition to GABAA receptors, metabotropic GABAB receptor activation can occur during synchronized and/or long-lasting activation of GABAergic inputs (Dutar and Nicoll, 1988; Isaacson et al., 1993; Mody et al., 1994; Scanziani, 2000; Thomson and Destexhe, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NGFCs form a large subset of interneuron population in the neocortex.
source: Among the various interneuron subtypes identified in the neocortex neurogliaform cells (NGFCs) form a large subset of interneuron population (Ascoli et al., 2008; Markram et al., 2004; Schuman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NGFCs form dense axonal arborization with an unusually high presynaptic bouton density that is highly interconnected with other neighboring neurons.
source: Compared to other interneuron subtypes, NGFCs form dense axonal arborization with an unusually high presynaptic bouton density that is highly interconnected with other neighboring neurons.
evidence: This statement describes a structural characteristic of NGFCs based on established knowledge.

claim: NGFCs are especially effective in recruiting metabotropic GABAB receptors in addition to ionotropic GABAA receptors by sporadic firing using single cell triggered volume transmission.
source: NGFCs are known to be especially effective in recruiting metabotropic GABAB receptors in addition to ionotropic GABAA receptors by sporadic firing using single cell triggered volume transmission in the microcircuit (Oláh et al., 2009; Tamás et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GABA binding to GABAB receptors catalyzes GDP/GTP exchange at the Gα subunit and the separation of Gβγ.
source: GABA binding to GABAB receptors catalyzes GDP/GTP exchange at the Gα subunit and the separation of Gβγ (Bettler et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim describes a molecular mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: Up to four Gβγ subunits bind cooperatively to GIRK channels and trigger a channel opening that drives the membrane potential toward the K+ reverse potential.
source: The Gβγ subunits – as membrane-anchored proteins – locally diffuse in the plasma membrane and up to four Gβγ subunits bind cooperatively to G-protein gated inward rectifier potassium (GIRK) channels and trigger a channel opening that drives the membrane potential toward the K+ reverse potential (Dascal, 1997; Inanobe and Kurachi, 2014; Stanfield et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2016; Wickman and Clapham, 1995).
evidence: This claim describes a molecular mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activation of GABAB receptors by NGFCs controls the firing of dendritic spikes in the distal dendritic domain in pyramidal cells.
source: Activation of GABAB receptors by NGFCs controls the firing of dendritic spikes in the distal dendritic domain in pyramidal cells (PCs) (Larkum et al., 1999; Palmer et al., 2012a; Wozny and Williams, 2011) and activity in the prefrontal cortex is effectively controlled by the strong feed-forward GABAB inhibition mediated by NGFCs (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Activity in the prefrontal cortex is effectively controlled by the strong feed-forward GABAB inhibition mediated by NGFCs.
source: Activation of GABAB receptors by NGFCs controls the firing of dendritic spikes in the distal dendritic domain in pyramidal cells (PCs) (Larkum et al., 1999; Palmer et al., 2012a; Wozny and Williams, 2011) and activity in the prefrontal cortex is effectively controlled by the strong feed-forward GABAB inhibition mediated by NGFCs (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GABAB receptors contribute to termination of persistent cortical activity.
source: Moreover, GABAB receptors contribute to termination of persistent cortical activity (Craig et al., 2013) and slow inhibition contributes to theta oscillations in the hippocampus (Capogna and Pearce, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Slow inhibition contributes to theta oscillations in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, GABAB receptors contribute to termination of persistent cortical activity (Craig et al., 2013) and slow inhibition contributes to theta oscillations in the hippocampus (Capogna and Pearce, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The estimated mean number of functional release sites (Nfrs) was 10.96 ± 8.1 with a mean quantal size (q) of 3.93 ± 1.21 pA.
source: According to BQA, the estimated mean Nfrs was 10.96 ± 8.1 with a mean quantal size (q) of 3.93 ± 1.21 pA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian quantal analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Direct synaptic junctions are not required for functional NGFC to PC connections.
source: Previous experiments showed that direct synaptic junctions are not required for functional NGFC to PC connections (Oláh et al., 2009) and GABA reaches receptors up to 3 µm from the release site (Farrant and Nusser, 2005; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Overstreet et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GABA reaches receptors up to 3 µm from the release site.
source: Previous experiments showed that direct synaptic junctions are not required for functional NGFC to PC connections (Oláh et al., 2009) and GABA reaches receptors up to 3 µm from the release site (Farrant and Nusser, 2005; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Overstreet et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The effective range of nonsynaptic volume transmission from NGFCs to PCs is 0.86–1.75 µm.
source: Projecting the range of BQA-derived Nfrs estimates over the number of NGFC boutons putatively involved in transmission for the same connections (Figure 1H, red lines) suggests an effective range of 0.86–1.75 µm for nonsynaptic volume transmission from NGFCs to PCs supporting previous reports on distances covered by extrasynaptic GABAergic communication (Farrant and Nusser, 2005; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Overstreet et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1H and supported by citations.

claim: Linear correlation (r = 0.863, p = 0.027) was detected between BQA-derived Nfrs and the number of NGFC boutons putatively involved in transmission at radial distances <1.5 µm from PC dendrites.
source: Moreover, we detected linear correlation (r = 0.863, p = 0.027) between BQA-derived Nfrs and the number of NGFC boutons putatively involved in transmission at radial distances <1.5 µm from PC dendrites; decreasing or increasing the distance resulted in the loss of correlation (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Interbouton distances were 3.36 ± 2.54 µm along reconstructed axons of NGFCs.
source: We also assessed the distance between axonal boutons (n = 1456) along reconstructed axons of NGFCs (n = 6) and found that interbouton distances were 3.36 ± 2.54 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from anatomical reconstructions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: α-actinin2 immunolabeling labels the overwhelming majority of supragranular NGFCs in the neocortex.
source: In order to achieve a relatively complete representation of all NGFC axon terminals in a model at the population level, we performed immunhistochemical labeling of α-actinin2, which is known to label the overwhelming majority of supragranular NGFCs in the neocortex (Uematsu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Less than eight NGFC axonal terminals contributed as effective GABA sources at any location in the superficial neocortex.
source: Using these conditions in simulations (n = 36), less than eight NGFC axonal terminals contributed as effective GABA sources at any location in the superficial neocortex (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When all putative NGFCs were active, most frequently a single NGFC release site serves as a GABA source (67.7 ± 7%).
source: Moreover, these boutons originated from a limited number of presynaptic NGFCs; when considering the extreme case of population-level cooperativity, that is, when all putative NGFCs were active, most frequently a single NGFC release site serves as a GABA source (67.7 ± 7%) and potential interactions between two, three, or more different NGFCs take place in limited occasions (15.34 ± 2.1%, 8.5 ± 2.6%, and 8.45 ± 3.16%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Potential interactions between two different NGFCs take place in 15.34 ± 2.1% of occasions.
source: Moreover, these boutons originated from a limited number of presynaptic NGFCs; when considering the extreme case of population-level cooperativity, that is, when all putative NGFCs were active, most frequently a single NGFC release site serves as a GABA source (67.7 ± 7%) and potential interactions between two, three, or more different NGFCs take place in limited occasions (15.34 ± 2.1%, 8.5 ± 2.6%, and 8.45 ± 3.16%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Transcallosal fibers establish interhemispheric inhibition that operates via GABAB receptor activation located on apical dendrites.
source: Transcallosal fibers establish interhemispheric inhibition that operates via GABAB receptor activation located on apical dendrites (Palmer et al., 2012b) and it has been suggested that this massive GABAB receptor recruitment in the superficial layers includes the activation of NGFCs (Palmer et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Massive GABAB receptor recruitment in the superficial layers includes the activation of NGFCs.
source: Transcallosal fibers establish interhemispheric inhibition that operates via GABAB receptor activation located on apical dendrites (Palmer et al., 2012b) and it has been suggested that this massive GABAB receptor recruitment in the superficial layers includes the activation of NGFCs (Palmer et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: On average, 38.2 ± 5.2% of the L1 neurons were active following ipsilateral hindlimb stimulation.
source: On average, 38.2 ± 5.2% of the L1 neurons were active following ipsilateral hindlimb stimulation, which is remarkably similar to the proportion found earlier (Palmer et al., 2012b; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The majority of the active neurons were α-actinin2 positive (10 out of 15 neurons, 67%).
source: Cross-examination of neurons responsive/non-responsive to hindlimb stimulation versus neurons immunopositive/negative for α-actinin2 revealed that the majority of the active neurons were α-actinin2 positive (10 out of 15 neurons, 67%, n = 2 animals) and the majority of inactive neurons were α-actinin2 negative (22 out of 26 neurons, 85%, Figure 3G) suggesting that a substantial fraction of L1 NGFCs are activated during hindlimb stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The majority of inactive neurons were α-actinin2 negative (22 out of 26 neurons, 85%).
source: Cross-examination of neurons responsive/non-responsive to hindlimb stimulation versus neurons immunopositive/negative for α-actinin2 revealed that the majority of the active neurons were α-actinin2 positive (10 out of 15 neurons, 67%, n = 2 animals) and the majority of inactive neurons were α-actinin2 negative (22 out of 26 neurons, 85%, Figure 3G) suggesting that a substantial fraction of L1 NGFCs are activated during hindlimb stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A substantial fraction of L1 NGFCs are activated during hindlimb stimulation.
source: Cross-examination of neurons responsive/non-responsive to hindlimb stimulation versus neurons immunopositive/negative for α-actinin2 revealed that the majority of the active neurons were α-actinin2 positive (10 out of 15 neurons, 67%, n = 2 animals) and the majority of inactive neurons were α-actinin2 negative (22 out of 26 neurons, 85%, Figure 3G) suggesting that a substantial fraction of L1 NGFCs are activated during hindlimb stimulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunohistochemistry and imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Smaller and bigger inputs in a triplet were −1.68 ± 1.51 and −2.19 ± 1.33 mV, respectively.
source: First, we measured the amplitude of unitary IPSPs (n = 8) elicited by single L1 NGFCs in the target L2/3 PC and found that smaller and bigger inputs in a triplet were −1.68 ± 1.51 and −2.19 ± 1.33 mV (rise time: 4.66 ± 2 ms; half-width: 19.29 ± 5.76 ms; decay time: 8.94 ± 2.91 ms), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from triple recordings.

claim: Coactivation of two L1 NGFC inputs resulted in moderately sublinear summation of convergent IPSPs (maximal nonlinearity, −9.1 ± 4.3%).
source: Next we activated the two L1 NGFC inputs synchronously (0.17 ± 0.05 ms) and such coactivation resulted in moderately sublinear summation of convergent IPSPs (maximal nonlinearity, −9.1 ± 4.3%) measured as the difference of calculated (−3.81 ± 2.76 mV) and experimentally determined (−3.57 ± 2.55 mV) sums of convergent single inputs (n = 4, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The time course of sublinearity followed the fast, presumably GABAA receptor-mediated part of the unitary and summated IPSPs.
source: Interestingly, the time course of sublinearity followed the fast, presumably GABAA receptor-mediated part of the unitary and summated IPSPs (Figure 4C) suggesting that ionotropic and metabotropic GABAergic components of the same input combinations might follow different rules of summation.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ionotropic and metabotropic GABAergic components of the same input combinations might follow different rules of summation.
source: Interestingly, the time course of sublinearity followed the fast, presumably GABAA receptor-mediated part of the unitary and summated IPSPs (Figure 4C) suggesting that ionotropic and metabotropic GABAergic components of the same input combinations might follow different rules of summation.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Peak amplitudes of converging smaller and bigger slow IPSPs were −0.66±0.22 and −0.94±0.37 mV, respectively.
source: Peak amplitudes of converging smaller and bigger slow IPSPs were −0.66±0.22 and −0.94±0.37 mV, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from triple recordings in gabazine.

claim: Synchronous activation of two presynaptic L1 NGFC converging onto the same L2/3 PC resulted in linear (−1.6 ± 6.6%) summation of slow IPSPs.
source: Synchronous activation of two presynaptic L1 NGFC converging onto the same L2/3 PC resulted in linear (−1.6 ± 6.6%) summation of slow IPSPs as peak amplitudes of calculated sums of individual inputs versus experimentally recorded compound responses were −1.58 ± 0.53 and −1.60 ± 0.55 mV, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings in gabazine shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Triple recordings in gabazine versus control conditions suggest significantly different (p = 0.021, two-sided MW U-test) linear interactions between slow, GABAB IPSPs as opposed to sublinearly summating fast, GABAA IPSPs.
source: Taken together, our triple recordings in gabazine versus control conditions suggest significantly different (p = 0.021, two-sided MW U-test) linear interactions between slow, GABAB IPSPs as opposed to sublinearly summating fast, GABAA IPSPs elicited by the same presynaptic interneuron population.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data from triple recordings.

claim: The distal apical dendritic membrane of PCs express voltage-dependent hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 1 (HCN1) known to attenuate dendritic signals.
source: The predominant target area of the superficial NGFCs, the distal apical dendritic membrane of PCs, express voltage-dependent hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 1 (HCN1) known to attenuate dendritic signals (Berger et al., 2001; Kalmbach et al., 2018; Lörincz et al., 2002; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003; Sheets et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Recordings in the presence of HCN1 channel blocker, ZD7288 showed summation properties similar to control.
source: Importantly, recordings in the presence of HCN1 channel blocker, ZD7288 (10 µM) showed summation properties similar to control, summation was linear with two APs and changed to slightly sublinear upon the 3rd to 4th spike (n = 5, 1AP: −0.82 ± 0.63 mV, 2APs: −1.59 ± 0.76 mV, 3APs: −1.66 ± 0.72 mV, 4APs: −1.90 ± 1.07 mV, unitary IPSP rise time: 97.7 ± 29.05 ms and decay time: 103.57 ± 48.94 ms; Figure 5B; normalized values and its comparison to control: 2APs: 2.06 ± 1.06, p = 0.983; 3APs: 1.99 ± 1.17, p = 0.362; 4APs: 2.56 ± 1.6, p = 0.336; two-sided MW U-test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: When a physiologically probable number of NGFCs are simultaneously active, HCN1 channels are locally not recruited to interfere with the summation of GABAB receptor-mediated responses.
source: These experiments suggest that when a physiologically probable number of NGFCs are simultaneously active, HCN1 channels are locally not recruited to interfere with the summation of GABAB receptor-mediated responses.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Extracellular GABA concentration producing GABAB receptor activation is tightly regulated via GABA transporters (GAT-1).
source: Previous experiments suggested that a single AP in an NGFC is able to fill the surrounding extracellular space with an effective concentration of GABA (Oláh et al., 2009) and, in turn, extracellular GABA concentration producing GABAB receptor activation is tightly regulated via GABA transporters (GAT-1) (Gonzalez-Burgos et al., 2009; Isaacson et al., 1993; Rózsa et al., 2017; Szabadics et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Selective blockade of GAT-1 with NO-711 increased the amplitude of GABAB receptor-mediated IPSP but did not influence summation properties.
source: Selective blockade of GAT-1 with NO-711 (10 µM) increased the amplitude of GABAB receptor-mediated IPSP; however, it did not influence summation properties (n = 6, 1AP: −1.11 ± 0.62 mV, 2APs: −2.28 ± 1.07 mV, 3APs: −3.1 ± 0.40 mV, 4APs: −3.54 ± 1.59 mV, unitary IPSP rise time: 118.85 ± 37.58 ms; decay time: 80.54 ± 40.94 ms; Figure 5B; normalized values and its comparison to control: 2APs: 2.06 ± 1.17, p = 0.853; 3APs: 2.36 ± 0.31, p = 0.645; 4APs: 2.97 ± 1.54, p = 0.515; two-sided MW U-test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Interactions between an in vivo realistic number of simultaneously active NGFCs lead to linear GABAB response summation even if increased concentration of GABA is present in the extracellular space.
source: Accordingly, interactions between an in vivo realistic number of simultaneously active NGFCs lead to linear GABAB response summation even if increased concentration of GABA is present in the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from experimental data.

claim: GABAB receptors and GIRK channels are segregated on dendritic shafts.
source: High-resolution quantitative electron microscopy showed that GABAB receptors and GIRK channels are segregated on dendritic shafts; however, receptor-channel complexes colocalize on dendritic spines (Kulik et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Receptor-channel complexes colocalize on dendritic spines.
source: High-resolution quantitative electron microscopy showed that GABAB receptors and GIRK channels are segregated on dendritic shafts; however, receptor-channel complexes colocalize on dendritic spines (Kulik et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The distance between the receptor and effector limits the recruitment of effector molecules to the vicinity of receptors.
source: Theoretical studies suggest that the distance between the receptor and effector limits the recruitment of effector molecules to the vicinity of receptors (Brinkerhoff et al., 2008; Kulik et al., 2006), thus we asked if summation properties were influenced by the relative location of of GABAB receptors and GIRK channels when several presynaptic inputs converge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical studies.

claim: Single AP triggered GABA release can activate a total of 5.82 ± 2.43 GABAB receptors (2.81 ± 1.55 on spine, 3.01 ± 1.71 on the shaft).
source: Our modeling trials show that single AP triggered GABA release can activate a total of 5.82 ± 2.43 GABAB receptors (2.81 ± 1.55 on spine, 3.01 ± 1.71 on the shaft).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Activation of GABAB receptors triggers intracellular mechanisms and produces Gβγ subunits (peak number of Gβγ subunits for single AP: 338.54 ± 138.75).
source: Furthermore, activation of GABAB receptors triggers intracellular mechanisms and the initial GDP/GTP exchange at the Gα subunit separates the G-protein heterotrimeric protein and produces Gβγ subunits (peak number of Gβγ subunits for single AP: 338.54 ± 138.75).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Lateral membrane diffusion of Gβγ subunits lead to the activation of 3.66 ± 2.17 GIRK channels in total (2.47 ± 1.88 on spine, 1.17 ± 1.26 on the shaft) in response to single AP.
source: Lateral membrane diffusion of Gβγ subunits lead to the activation of 3.66 ± 2.17 GIRK channels in total (2.47 ± 1.88 on spine, 1.17 ± 1.26 on the shaft) in response to single AP.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Two consecutive APs resulted in the activation of 6.98 ± 3.29 GIRK channels (2.13 ± 1.63 on dendritic shaft and 4.85 ± 2.65 on spine).
source: Two consecutive APs resulted in the activation of 6.98 ± 3.29 GIRK channels (2.13 ± 1.63 on dendritic shaft and 4.85 ± 2.65 on spine) in the simulations.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The number of activated GIRK channels in response to two APs was close to the arithmetic sum of the number of GIRK channels activated by two single AP responses (−4.87% in total, −1.86% on spines and −9.86% on the shaft).
source: Importantly, this number of activated GIRK channels in response to two APs was close to the arithmetic sum of the number of GIRK channels activated by two single AP responses (−4.87% in total, −1.86% on spines and −9.86% on the shaft; Figures 4E and 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figures 4E and 5A.

claim: Spines represent the preferred site of action for GABAB receptor-GIRK channel signaling.
source: The compartment-specific effectiveness of signaling as the ratio of activated GIRK channels and active GABAB receptors (Figure 6F) shows that spines represent the preferred site of action corroborating earlier suggestions (Qian and Sejnowski, 1990).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 6F and supported by a citation.

claim: NGFC activation generates an unusually prolonged inhibition on the postsynaptic cell.
source: Numerous observations support the idea of volume transmission (Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015). (1) NGFC activation generates an unusually prolonged inhibition on the postsynaptic cell (Karayannis et al., 2010; Mańko et al., 2012; Oláh et al., 2009; Szabadics et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Released GABA acts on synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA receptors.
source: (2) Released GABA acts on synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA receptors (Karayannis et al., 2010; Oláh et al., 2009; Price et al., 2005; Tamás et al., 2003), (3) as well as on nearby presynaptic terminals (Oláh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Released GABA acts on nearby presynaptic terminals.
source: (2) Released GABA acts on synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA receptors (Karayannis et al., 2010; Oláh et al., 2009; Price et al., 2005; Tamás et al., 2003), (3) as well as on nearby presynaptic terminals (Oláh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NGFCs show a very high rate of functional coupling between the neighboring neurons.
source: (4) NGFCs show a very high rate of functional coupling between the neighboring neurons (Jiang et al., 2015; Oláh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ultrastructural observations showed the lack of clearly defined postsynaptic elements in the apposition of the NGFC boutons.
source: (5) Ultrastructural observations showed the lack of clearly defined postsynaptic elements in the apposition of the NGFC boutons (Mańko et al., 2012; Oláh et al., 2009; Vida et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NGFCs act on astrocytes within the reach of their axonal arborization through nonsynaptic coupling.
source: (6) NGFCs act on astrocytes within the reach of their axonal arborization through nonsynaptic coupling (Rózsa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GABA released from NGFC axonal terminals activates GABA receptors up to about ~1.8 µm.
source: Here, we used functional and structural characterization of NGFC-PC inhibitory connections and suggest that GABA released from NGFC axonal terminals activates GABA receptors up to about ~1.8 µm, a result remarkably similar to previous estimations for the range of extrasynaptic action of synaptically released GABA (Farrant and Nusser, 2005; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015; Overstreet et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on functional and structural characterization presented in the manuscript and supported by citations.

claim: The overwhelming majority of the superficial cortical space is effectively covered by at least one NGFC.
source: Although the concept of blanket inhibition has been suggested for networks of interneuron populations having overlapping axonal arborizations and dense synaptic output (Karnani et al., 2014), our spatial model based on high-resolution reconstructions of labeled NGFCs takes the concept to its extremes and reveals an unprecedented density of release sites for a population of cortical neuron and shows that the overwhelming majority of the superficial cortical space is effectively covered by at least one NGFC.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results incorporating experimental data.

claim: A single cortical spatial voxel is reached by GABA released from a limited number of individual NGFCs, ~83% of space is covered by one or two NGFCs.
source: At the same time, the redundancy of the NGFC population is limited and a single cortical spatial voxel is reached by GABA released from a limited number of individual NGFCs, ~83% of space is covered by one or two NGFCs.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results incorporating experimental data.

claim: Strong cholinergic neuromodulation of NGFCs and frequent gap junctional coupling between NGFCs further facilitate concerted action.
source: Strong cholinergic neuromodulation of NGFCs (Poorthuis et al., 2018) and frequent gap junctional coupling between NGFCs (Simon et al., 2005) further facilitate concerted action and are likely to play a major role in synchronizing the NGFC network (Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct measurements of two converging NGFC inputs on L2/3 PC from simultaneous triple whole-cell patch clamp recordings revealed sublinear summation properties for ionotropic GABAA receptor-mediated responses.
source: When studying simultaneous action of NGFCs, our direct measurements of two converging NGFC inputs on L2/3 PC from simultaneous triple whole-cell patch clamp recordings revealed sublinear summation properties for ionotropic GABAA receptor-mediated responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings.

claim: Mechanisms of interaction between convergent inputs from NGFCs might be similar to those suggested for short-term synaptic depression of GABAA responses such as local drops in Cl− driving force and membrane conductance.
source: Mechanisms of interaction between convergent inputs from NGFCs might be similar to those suggested for short-term synaptic depression of GABAA responses such as local drops in Cl− driving force and membrane conductance (Huguenard and Alger, 1986; McCarren and Alger, 1985; Staley and Proctor, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculation based on inference and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The simultaneous triple recordings of two presynaptic NGFCs targeting the same postsynaptic PC represent the first direct experimental attempt addressing the summation of metabotropic receptor-mediated postsynaptic interactions.
source: To our knowledge, the simultaneous triple recordings of two presynaptic NGFCs targeting the same postsynaptic PC represent the first direct experimental attempt addressing the summation of metabotropic receptor-mediated postsynaptic interactions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Scarce computational model studies suggested a highly supralinear interaction through the amplification effect of G-protein cooperativity.
source: To date, scarce computational model studies were aimed to explore the integration properties of GABAB receptor-mediated responses and suggested a highly supralinear interaction through the amplification effect of G-protein cooperativity (Destexhe and Sejnowski, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous computational work.

claim: The experimental approach indicates linear interactions between GABAB receptor-mediated responses in case the number of converging presynaptic cells corresponds to the number of NGFCs cooperating during in vivo network operations.
source: Our experimental approach indicates linear interactions between GABAB receptor-mediated responses in case the number of converging presynaptic cells corresponds to the number of NGFCs cooperating during in vivo network operations.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Converging afferents that act on inhibitory metabotropic receptors in the same postsynaptic voxel show linear or slightly sublinear summation, conserving the impact of individual inputs.
source: This suggests that converging afferents that act on inhibitory metabotropic receptors in the same postsynaptic voxel show linear or slightly sublinear summation, conserving the impact of individual inputs.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from experimental findings.

claim: Summation properties in response to synchronized inputs from NGFCs are not significantly affected by HCN1 channels.
source: Our experiments presented above show that summation properties in response to synchronized inputs from NGFCs are not significantly affected by HCN1 channels, presumably due to the relatively moderate local hyperpolarization arriving from NGFCs; again, further studies are needed to test the influence of additional interneuron classes coactivated together with NGFCs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The density and distribution of neocortical NGFCs and their axonal terminals combined with the effective range of GABAergic volume transmission appear optimized for a spatially ubiquitous and predominantly linear metabotropic GABAB receptor summation.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the density and distribution of neocortical NGFCs and their axonal terminals combined with the effective range of GABAergic volume transmission appear optimized for a spatially ubiquitous and predominantly linear metabotropic GABAB receptor summation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the integration of experimental and modeling results.
